subject: Critical Thinking
title: SIFT Method: A Quick Source Evaluation Framework
description: A fast breakdown of SIFT Method: A Quick Source Evaluation Framework for builders.

hook.text: You see a shocking claim online. In 30 seconds, you can determine if it's worth your attention.

buildup.text: SIFT: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace the original claim. Four steps, 30 seconds.

discovery.text: Mike Caulfield developed SIFT for digital literacy. It's used by universities and fact-checkers worldwide.

twist.text: The crucial step is STOP. Most people react first and think later. The pause before sharing is the most valuable second.

climax.text: Finding better coverage means: search for the same claim in trusted sources.

punchline.text: Stop. Investigate. Find. Trace. Thirty seconds to separate signal from noise.

quiz.question: What does the 'S' in SIFT stand for?
options: Stop — pause before reacting to a claim

details.summary: SIFT stands for Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace to the original. This quick lateral-reading method helps you evaluate online claims in under 60 seconds without needing deep expertise in the topic.
details.whyItMatters: SIFT provides a practical, fast method for evaluating claims when you encounter them in the wild rather than in a classroom or research context.
takeaways: Stop before engaging with or sharing the content
Investigate the source before evaluating the claim
Find better coverage from more reliable sources for the same topic

faq.question: How does the SIFT method differ from traditional source evaluation?
faq.answer: Traditional evaluation reads deeply within a source. SIFT uses lateral reading — quickly leaving the page to check what others say about the source. This is faster and often more reliable because it leverages the broader information ecosystem rather than analyzing one source in isolation.

faq.question: Can you walk through the SIFT method with a practical example?
faq.answer: You see a health claim shared on social media. Stop: do not share yet. Investigate: look up the website sharing it. Find better coverage: search for the same claim on medical news sites. Trace: find the original study. This process takes under 60 seconds.
